title: Game console and controller: batteries, fan, heatsink, drive and magnets
summary: Home consoles give a big heatsink and fan, a disc drive, a hard drive with magnets and an internal power supply; controllers and handhelds give lithium cells, rumble motors and sometimes Hall sensors. Allow about 30 minutes. Cases use security screws, the cells can catch fire, the power supply keeps its charge and the disc drive has a laser.

steps.text: Unplug the power lead and every other cable, then wait 10 minutes. If a disc is stuck in the drive, don't force the tray: most drives have a small manual-release hole beside the slot or tray that you can poke with a straightened paper clip.

Deal with the batteries first. Open the battery covers on controllers and take the cells out. Handhelds and some controllers hold a sealed lithium pack inside: look for a bulging back, a gap along the seam or a lifted screen. Take any swollen one outdoors and read safety_swollen_lithium before going on.

Open a controller: take out the screws on the back (Phillips, or tri-wing or security Torx on some), then run a plastic pry tool round the seam. Lift the halves apart slowly: ribbon and battery cables join the two sides. Photograph the layout.

Disconnect the controller's lithium pack by its plug, or cut one lead at a time and tape each end. Lift out the two rumble motors (small cylinders with an off-centre weight and two wires each), the thumbsticks and the triggers. Keep the sticks and triggers whole: the Hall-effect sensors in many are tiny chips that are hard to unsolder.
steps.warn: A short across a lithium pack can make wire glow and start a fire. Never cut both leads at once, and tape each end the moment it's cut.

steps.text: Home console: peel off the rubber feet and stickers to find hidden screws, take them all out (often Torx or tri-wing) and release the clips round the seam with a plastic pry tool. Keep the screws in a labelled tray as you go: lengths differ.
Unplug the fan's connector from the board and undo its screws. A console fan is a 12 V blower or axial fan, strong and quiet. Keep it with its plug.

Lift out the disc drive: unplug its ribbon and power lead, undo the 3-4 screws and slide it out in one piece. Keep it closed. Strip it later with teardown_optical_drive if you want its motors and pickup.
steps.warn: The laser in a Blu-ray or DVD drive can hurt your eyes even when it seems dark. Never power an open drive and never look into the lens.

steps.text: Unscrew the hard drive from its caddy (usually 4 screws) and keep it whole. It holds strong neodymium magnets: see teardown_hard_drive to get them out safely.

Remove the internal power supply (a metal box or board where the mains lead plugs in): unplug its cables and take out its screws. Don't open it. If you want it open, wait several days, then discharge its big capacitors (see safety_discharge_capacitor) and check for under 1 V.
steps.warn: The supply's capacitors can hold hundreds of volts long after it was unplugged. Don't touch the board or bare metal inside it.

steps.text: Remove the heatsink from the main chip: undo its 4-8 spring-loaded screws a turn at a time in a criss-cross order, then twist gently to break the dried paste before lifting. Don't bend or cut the heat pipes. Wipe off the paste.

Unscrew the motherboard and lift it out. Keep it whole as a source of connectors, capacitors, inductors and regulators for later (see skill_soldering). The big chips are no use on their own. Bag it and write on the bag what it came from.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Batteries.** Controller and handheld packs are 3.7-7.7 V, about 500 mAh in a pad up to 5 Ah in a handheld. Many pads use AA cells instead. Test the lithium cells before use (see test_lithium_cell) and keep the protection board with them.
- **Fan and heatsink.** A 12 V fan is a strong airflow source for a dehydrator, forge blower or cooler. The big copper and aluminium heatsink spreads heat from a power part, or carries the cold side of a thermoelectric cooler (see build_peltier_cooler).
- **Rumble motors.** Small 3-5 V DC motors with an off-centre weight. Remove the weight for a smooth little motor, or keep them as vibration alarms.
- **Magnets.** From the internal hard drive. See teardown_hard_drive.
- **Hall sensors.** Detect a magnet's position: use them as door and lid sensors, or as speed pickups.
- **Power supply.** Many consoles have a 12 V supply of 8-20 A inside. Once discharged and fitted back in a closed box it makes a bench supply. Treat it as a mains device and never run it open.
- **Laser pickup.** Leave it sealed. The diode is tiny and dangerous without proper goggles.

## Variations

- Older consoles (Atari, NES, Mega Drive and the like) use external adapters and have no drive: just a board, a case and controller ports.
- Handhelds (Switch, Steam Deck and similar) pack a screen, a big lithium pack and Hall-effect sticks into one case. The pack may be glued down: use plastic tools only and never bend it.
- Some controllers have a charging port and a small charging chip on the board.

## What to leave

- Swollen batteries and any battery under about 2 V.
- The power supply's capacitors, unless you have discharged them.
- The plastic shell.
